topic: Empirical study of harness design for coding agents: how much does the harness matter?

primary_sources.title: An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents (arXiv:2609.20804v1, 17 Sep 2026)
primary_sources.why: Anchor study for this article. Fixed execution loop, varied three components (planning, action space, context management) across 4 models x 2 benchmarks = 176 matched settings.

primary_sources.title: Claw-SWE-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating OpenClaw-style Agent Harnesses on Coding Tasks (10 Jun 2026)
primary_sources.why: Harness as a controlled experimental variable; 350 tasks, 8 languages, 43 repos; adapter swap 19.1% -> 73.4%.

primary_sources.title: Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness (position paper)
primary_sources.why: Binding Constraint Thesis + public-leaderboard evidence (SEAL vs Claude Code, HAL cross-scaffold swings).

primary_sources.title: CliffCompaction: Cost-Efficient Compaction for Long-Horizon Coding Agents (22 Sep 2026)
primary_sources.why: Counterpoint to LLM summarization: truncate/drop only, never summarize a summary; up to 50% cost cut.

primary_sources.title: Harness Engineering: Anatomy, Architecture, and Evolution of Coding Agents - A Source-Code Study of Eleven Systems (15 Jul 2026)
primary_sources.why: Definitions/subsystems baseline across 11 production harnesses; 29 recurring design patterns.

primary_sources.title: Harness engineering for coding agent users (Birgitta Boeckeler, 02 Apr 2026)
primary_sources.why: The user-side harness framing: guides (feedforward) vs sensors (feedback); harnessability of a codebase.

primary_sources.title: Six Agent Harness Capabilities for Higher Model Performance (NVIDIA)
primary_sources.why: Pass-by-reference tool results remove the need for compaction; 82.2% SWE-bench Verified with GPT-5.5 at ~half tokens/calls.

primary_sources.title: The Coding Harness Behind GitHub Copilot in VS Code (15 May 2026)
primary_sources.why: Vendor-side anatomy: context assembly, tool exposure, agent loop, round vs turn.

key_points: Ranks top for the anchor paper query; AI overview states no component works the same way across all models and tasks.
Explains the two-threshold compaction design (soft threshold -> stubs with originals on disk; hard threshold -> oldest middle events folded into a running summary).
Stresses that fewer than 3% of runs ended without editing code regardless of planning, so planning was not rescuing stalled attempts but trimming repetition after the fix existed.
Frames the takeaway as 'the right harness matches the failure mode' rather than more scaffolding being better.
Agent = Model + Harness; narrows the term to two bounded contexts (built-in harness vs the outer harness users build around a coding agent).
Split into guides (feedforward controls) and sensors (feedback controls); the strongest sensors emit LLM-optimized signals such as linters that include self-correction instructions.
Introduces harnessability: strongly typed languages, clear module boundaries and opinionated frameworks raise an agent's chance of success.
Quotes OpenAI's harness-engineering report: layered architecture enforced by custom linters and structural tests plus recurring 'garbage collection' for drift.
The single best synthesis of the 2026 numbers: model-paper advances move scores 2-4 points while harness swaps moved them 6-54.

Reports a controlled factorial (Zhang et al.) where harness-induced variance exceeded model-induced variance by 7.8x on a SWE-bench subset, with 6 of 9 model-pair rankings reversing under a different scaffold.
Explains why the harness has headroom: a weak harness raises per-step difficulty repeatedly across a long loop; the ceiling is set by how badly the harness sabotages the model.

Documents AHE harness self-evolution: 69.7% -> 77.0% on Terminal-Bench 2 with a frozen model, transfer to other models, and an ablation where system-prompt edits actually cost 2.3 points while memory (+5.6), tools (+3.3) and middleware (+2.2) paid off.
Names the real methodological sin: leaderboards report each model under its own best-tuned scaffold, which is neither a locked-harness comparison nor a factorial decomposition.
Ties three 2026 papers together (Claw-SWE-Bench, Harness-Bench, UTBoost) around the claim that the harness is at least as important as the model.
Harness choice 27.4pp vs model choice 29.4pp under identical conditions: nearly equal effects.
Harness-Bench: 5,194 trajectories, 106 sandboxed tasks; introduces 'execution-alignment failures' where plausible reasoning decouples from tool feedback and workspace state.
UTBoost: broken tests affected 40.9% of SWE-bench Lite entries and 24.4% of Verified entries, so the grading layer was also unmeasured.
Practical mapping to harness configuration flags (structured output schema as the evaluator contract).
Compaction timing lesson: Claude Code auto-compaction fires near 95% of the window, after the 'dumb zone' has already been reasoned in.
Manual compaction should trigger at phase transitions and before the hardest reasoning, with a focus directive to steer what survives.
Graduated stages beat one cliff (warn 70% -> mask 80% -> prune 85% -> aggressive mask 90% -> full summary 99%).
Offload before summarizing so compaction is recoverable rather than merely smaller; cites 91.6% completion for pruned+summarized context vs 71% full-context.

stats.fact: The controlled study evaluates 176 matched experimental settings across four models and two benchmarks: 22 settings per model-benchmark pair (20 context-management settings spanning five tiers T0-T4 at 32k/64k/96k/128k, plus one planning ablation and one bash-only ablation).

Models: Nemotron-3 30B, 120B and 550B plus Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B, served locally with SGLang BF16, temperature 0. Benchmarks: SWE-Bench Verified (500 human-verified GitHub issues) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (89 command-line tasks). At most 300 steps per task; 16,384 output tokens per turn; tool results truncated to 24k characters.

Context-management value is budget-dependent: the managed-minus-T0 success gap falls from 35.7pp to 15.9, 5.5 and 2.7pp across 32k/64k/96k/128k on SWE-Bench, and from 9.5 to 7.5, 4.8 and 2.8pp on Terminal-Bench.

Most of context management's benefit is overflow prevention: the unmanaged T0 window-overflow rate falls from 78.7% to 8.7% on SWE-Bench and 61.0% to 12.1% on Terminal-Bench as the budget grows, while every managed tier (T1-T4) overflows on exactly zero tasks at every budget.

Extreme budget sensitivity in the smallest model: Nemotron-3 30B scores 0% on SWE-Bench at 32k with no context management (T0) versus 20.6% with elision only (T1); the same model at 128k goes 24.8% (T0) vs 25.0% (T1).
Nemotron-3 550B on SWE-Bench at 32k: T0 0% vs T3 (summarization alone) 58.4% - a 58.4pp swing from one harness component at a tight budget.

Staged elision-then-summarization (T4) matches the accuracy of T1-T3 while posting the lowest cost in 7 of 8 model-benchmark panels and the lowest mean cost per task at every window budget; early cheap elision removes the need for many costly LLM summarization calls.

Recoverable context is dead weight: across 32 model-benchmark-window comparisons, T2 (elision + recall_event) beats T1 (elision alone) in 15 settings, loses in 14 and ties in 3, for an equal-weight mean difference of -0.36pp. 36 of 64 T2/T4 settings (56.3%) never call recall_event, the median invocation rate is zero, and mean calls per task fall from 0.540 at 32k to 0.069 / 0.011 / 0.007 at 64k/96k/128k.

Planning is an accuracy scaffold for weak models and a cost saver for strong ones: for Nemotron-3 30B it adds 11.6pp on SWE-Bench and 4.5pp on Terminal-Bench at higher cost; for Nemotron-3 550B and Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B it cuts SWE-Bench cost by roughly 30% and 32% while success drops 2.0pp and 0.4pp.

Mechanism behind the planning result: with planning off, 68.6% of Nemotron-3 30B SWE-Bench runs ended without an edit and 58.4% stalled in the Localize phase; with planning on those fall to 27.8% and 10.4%, while for the strongest models the removed turns are mostly post-edit verification.

Action space crossover: the predefined tool set raises success for Nemotron-3 30B by 15.0pp (SWE-Bench) and 10.1pp (Terminal-Bench); for Nemotron-3 550B bash-only wins by 3.6pp and 5.6pp while cutting cost 53% and 30%; Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B gains 23.2pp from the full tool set on SWE-Bench but gains 6.7pp from bash-only on Terminal-Bench.

Why bash-only breaks weak models: 66% of Nemotron-3 30B bash-only Terminal-Bench trajectories terminate after out-of-interface tool emissions (the model emits learned tool-call patterns the bash registry cannot resolve), shortening the average trajectory from 71 to 15 turns. Bash-only trajectories also issue 32% fewer calls on SWE-Bench and 24% fewer on Terminal-Bench, consistent with denser composite shell commands.

Trajectory-level signature of each component: context management extends execution trajectories (median lengths 20-30 turns unmanaged vs roughly 50-180 managed at 32k) without changing phase ordering or behavior; planning changes where trajectories stop; the action space changes the granularity at which code is written.
Adapter/harness swap on a frozen model: OpenClaw with a minimal direct-diff adapter scores 19.1% Pass@1 (67/350) while the full adapter reaches 73.4% (257/350) with the same GLM 5.1 backbone.

Effect sizes are comparable: under fixed models, model choice changes Pass@1 by 29.4pp and harness choice by 27.4pp across an OpenClaw x nine-model sweep and a five-claw x two-model sweep. Five claws on GLM 5.1 span 60.9%-73.4% (12.5pp); on Qwen 3.6-flash the spread is larger, 38.6%-66.0%.

Harness-only edits move scores without touching weights: Terminal-Bench 2 pass@1 rises 69.7% -> 77.0% while holding the model fixed, and third-party monitoring reports up to 15pp (Kimi K2 Thinking) and 11pp (GPT-5) of scaffold-only variation on SWE-bench Verified.
stats.source: arXiv 2605.23950 (Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness)

stats.fact: Same-model ranking instability: Claude Opus 4.5 reaches 45.9% on SWE-bench Pro under the standardized SEAL scaffold but 55.4% under Claude Code; HAL reports same-model cross-scaffold swings up to nearly 48pp on SWE-bench Verified Mini, versus only 4.9pp spanning six frontier models under the standardized scaffold.

Third-party benchmark tracking: LangChain moved Terminal-Bench from 52.8% to 66.5% (+13.7pp) by changing only the harness (system prompt, tool choice, execution flow) with the model fixed; Anthropic showed resource configuration alone swings scores about 6pp, and differences below 3pp are noise.
stats.source: nwyin/tau benchmarks-landscape (Terminal-Bench paper, LangChain and Anthropic reports)

stats.fact: Compaction counter-design: CliffCompaction cuts cost by up to 50% under a bounded context while maintaining or improving Terminal-Bench performance, and adds over 10pp on Terminal-Bench for less than the cost of two full-context runs. Its rule is to only truncate or drop content - never rephrase - and to never compact a compaction, discarding prior compacted output instead.

Source-code audit of eleven production coding harnesses (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Mistral Vibe, OpenHands, Aider, Mini-SWE-Agent, Hermes, Pi, OpenCode, OpenClaw): across roughly four million lines, no agent runtime imports a general-purpose agentic framework and none retrieves code with vector embeddings. Skills lead MCP in adoption (9/11 vs 8/11) and ACP ships in six systems. Outputs 13 observations, 29 recurring design patterns, 18 design recommendations and a 90-line minimum-viable-harness scaffold.

Minimalism baseline: mini-SWE-agent is roughly 100 lines of Python with bash as its only action space; it posted about 65% on SWE-bench Verified in mid-2025 and its docs report 74%+ with newer frontier models. In the Lita comparison it trails OpenHands by 3.2pp on Claude Sonnet 4 (64.8 vs 68.0) but by only 0.2pp on Claude Opus 4 (67.6 vs 67.8) - scaffolding's marginal value shrinks as model capability rises.
stats.source: mini-SWE-agent docs and Lita Table 2, as compiled in the mini-SWE-agent review article

stats.fact: Avoiding compaction entirely: NVIDIA's NOOA reports 82.2% on SWE-bench Verified with GPT-5.5 using roughly half the tokens and LLM calls of comparison harnesses, and needs no context compaction because tool results pass by reference instead of being serialized into the context window.
stats.source: NVIDIA Developer Blog, Six Agent Harness Capabilities for Higher Model Performance

stats.fact: Grading layer is also noisy: UTBoost found tests weak enough that wrong patches passed, with corrections affecting 40.9% of SWE-bench Lite entries and 24.4% of Verified entries - so a leaderboard number is model x harness x verifier, two of which are usually unreported.
stats.source: UTBoost (Yu et al., ACL 2025), summarized in the deepfeed and Daniel Vaughan analyses

angles: Component-level, not monolithic: the 2026 literature moved from 'does the harness matter' (yes, 27-54pp) to 'which component buys what, for which model, at which budget'. This article should be organized around the second question.

The budget is the hidden confounder: context management's measured value is mostly overflow prevention, so its ROI collapses to ~2.7-2.8pp once the window is large. Buy window capacity OR buy compaction machinery - paying for both is the common mistake.

Cost is the second axis nobody plots: staged elision-then-summarization wins on cost (not accuracy), and bash-only cuts cost 30-53% for capable models. An accuracy-only reading of the same tables produces the wrong design decision.

Measure your features before shipping them: recall_event was built, documented and almost never called (56.3% of settings never invoked it, median zero). Instrument invocation rates, not just outcomes.

Every component has a failure mode signature, not just a score: context management changes trajectory length, planning changes where trajectories stop, action space changes edit granularity. Debug with trajectory shape.

The crossover thresholds are capability- and task-shaped: predefined tools for weak bash control, bash-only for capable models on shell-centric tasks (Mistral flips sign between SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench). The same model can need opposite harnesses on different task types.

Reporting hygiene as the practical deliverable: publish model + harness + context budget + step budget together. Benchmarks conflate three factors (model, harness, verifier) and UTBoost showed the verifier was wrong for ~41% of SWE-bench Lite gradings.

The harness effect is large precisely because harnesses are immature; expect it to shrink as the easy sabotage gets engineered out - so build measurement capability, not a permanent 'best harness' claim.

faq: Is the harness more important than the model? It depends on the comparison regime: under a locked harness the model dominates, in a factorial over immature harnesses the harness term dominates (reported 7.8x on one SWE-bench subset), and public leaderboards report neither cleanly.

Should I keep my context window large or invest in compaction? The measured margin shrinks to 2.7-2.8pp by 128k on the reported benchmarks, so a large window can substitute for part of the machinery - but managed tiers had zero overflow failures at every budget while unmanaged ones still lost 8.7-12.1% of tasks at 128k.
Do I need a plan step? Only if the model abandons tasks too early; for stronger models planning mostly trims post-edit verification and lowers cost, with a small success-rate cost.

Should I give the agent predefined tools or just bash? Predefined tools for models with weak shell control (up to 15pp on the smallest model); bash-only for bash-capable models, especially on command-line-centric tasks (3.6-6.7pp better with 30-53% lower cost).
Is lossless context recall worth building? In the study, no: it moved accuracy by -0.36pp on average and was invoked in a minority of settings, with median zero calls.

Why did my agent get worse as the run got longer? Check the context before the model - trajectory-level analysis shows most degradation is trajectory length and compaction policy, not model capability.
writer_notes: Type=guide: lead with the harness-effect magnitude (19.1% -> 73.4% adapter swap and 27.4pp vs 29.4pp), then go component by component using the anchor study's four findings, each paired with its trajectory-level mechanism. Keep every number attributed inline (arXiv id + section/table). Include the cost column everywhere the accuracy number appears - cost is where the actionable decisions live. Use the design rulebook section as the practical payload, and the measurement section to cover harness disclosure, locked-harness vs factorial regimes, and UTBoost-style verifier noise. Do not claim a universal 'best harness': the anchor study explicitly limits its claims to the components and implementations it tested, single runs per setting, and planning/action-space ablations only at the T4/128k baseline.
